clinicalPearls: Dyspareunia is persistent or recurrent genital pain associated with sexual intercourse and is a common but frequently underreported complaint
A key clinical step is to localise the pain as superficial (at the entrance) or deep (with deep penetration), since this narrows the likely causes
Superficial pain often reflects vulvovaginal conditions such as atrophy, vestibulodynia, dermatoses, infection, or inadequate lubrication
Deep pain suggests pelvic pathology including endometriosis, pelvic inflammatory disease, adhesions, fibroids, or ovarian pathology
Postmenopausal dyspareunia is commonly due to genitourinary syndrome of menopause from oestrogen deficiency and responds well to local oestrogen and lubrication
Dyspareunia and vaginismus frequently coexist and reinforce each other, and both fall within genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder
A careful history and a gentle, systematic examination to reproduce and localise the pain are central to diagnosis
Management is directed at the identified cause and often combines physical treatment with attention to the anxiety and relationship consequences of chronic sexual pain
reference.pathophysiology: Dyspareunia is a symptom with diverse underlying mechanisms rather than a single disease. Superficial (entry) pain arises from disorders of the vulva and introitus: oestrogen-deficient atrophy thinning and drying the tissue, provoked vestibulodynia with localised hypersensitivity, inflammatory or infective vulvovaginitis, dermatoses, or insufficient arousal and lubrication. Deep (pelvic) pain results from structures reached during deep penetration, so endometriosis, chronic pelvic inflammatory disease, adhesions, fibroids, and ovarian or uterine pathology can generate pain when moved or compressed. Persistent pain from any of these causes commonly triggers protective pelvic floor muscle tension and anticipatory anxiety, so a peripheral organic problem can evolve into a mixed pain syndrome with secondary vaginismus, blurring the line between physical and psychological contributors.
additionalDifferentials: Pelvic inflammatory disease or pelvic adhesions
additionalInvestigations: Detailed history localising pain as superficial or deep and defining its timing and triggers
Careful genital and pelvic examination attempting to reproduce and localise the pain
Assessment for infection, atrophy, and vulval skin disease
Pelvic ultrasound and, where indicated, laparoscopy to evaluate deep pelvic causes such as endometriosis
Assessment of pelvic floor muscle tone and psychosexual contributors
redFlags: Postcoital bleeding or an abnormal pelvic mass suggesting significant gynaecological pathology
Features of endometriosis or pelvic inflammatory disease requiring directed investigation
History of sexual trauma needing sensitive, specialised support
Chronic pain driving significant psychological distress or relationship breakdown
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the underlying cause; menopausal atrophic dyspareunia responds very well to local oestrogen, infective and inflammatory causes resolve with treatment, and even complex or chronic pain often improves with a combined physical and psychosexual approach, though deep pain from conditions such as endometriosis may require longer-term management.
pitfalls: Failing to distinguish superficial from deep pain, leading to misdirected investigation
Overlooking easily treatable atrophic changes in postmenopausal women
Missing endometriosis or other pelvic pathology as a cause of deep dyspareunia
Neglecting the secondary pelvic floor tension and anxiety that perpetuate the pain
management: Localise the pain as superficial or deep and direct treatment at the specific identified cause
Treat genitourinary syndrome of menopause and atrophic dyspareunia with local (vaginal) oestrogen plus lubricants and moisturisers
Manage vulvovaginal infection, dermatoses and provoked vestibulodynia with targeted topical therapy and neuropathic agents for vestibulodynia
Address deep pain by treating the underlying pelvic pathology such as endometriosis, pelvic inflammatory disease or fibroids
Offer pelvic floor physiotherapy for coexisting muscle overactivity and vaginismus
Provide psychosexual counselling to address anticipatory anxiety and the mixed pain component that develops over time
Refer to a multidisciplinary team including gynaecology, dermatology, pain and psychosexual therapy for refractory or complex pain
